title: YouTube as a source of information on epidural steroid injection
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of the 50 most-viewed English-language YouTube videos on epidural steroid injection (search 13 February 2020). Two physiatrists classified each video as useful, misleading or neither against the Spine Intervention Society practice guidelines, where misleading required at least one inaccurate scientific or clinical statement: 8% (n = 4) were misleading. That is a share of items judged inaccurate against an external ground truth, so CONTENT. The paper's mDISCERN and GQS threshold shares are additionally recorded as QUALITY rows.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language YouTube videos; authors based in the Republic of Korea)
estimates.measure_type: % of the 50 most-viewed YouTube videos on epidural steroid injection classified as misleading
estimates.denominator: 50 most-viewed English-language YouTube videos whose primary content is epidural steroid injection, from searches on four keywords ('epidural injection', 'epidural steroid injection', 'epidural transforaminal injection', 'epidural transforaminal steroid injection'), duplicates and videos without audio excluded
estimates.definition: A video was classified as misleading if it contained at least one inaccurate scientific statement about the definition of ESI, at least one inaccurate statement about the pain-reducing mechanism of ESI, or at least one inaccurate clinical statement about the indications, adverse effects, benefits and potential outcomes of ESI. A video containing both accurate and inaccurate statements was classified as misleading.
estimates.misinfo_def: No definition of misinformation is given; the operational definition is the misleading-video criterion: "The criteria for misleading videos included 1) at least one inaccurate scientific statement about the definition of ESO [ESI]; 2) at least one inaccurate statement about the pain-reducing mechanism of ESI; or 3) at least one inaccurate clinical statement about the indications, adverse effects, benefits, and potential outcomes of ESI."
estimates.source_quote: 76% (n = 38) were classified as useful videos, and 8% (n = 4) as misleading videos. The other 16% (n = 8) were neither useful nor misleading videos.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 1355; also the Abstract and Discussion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two physical medicine and rehabilitation physicians (the two authors) assessed reliability, quality and usefulness of every video, with discrepancies discussed until consensus; assessment was based on the Spine Intervention Society's Practice Guidelines for Spinal Diagnostic and Treatment Procedures (Bogduk, 2nd ed., 2013). The authors state as a limitation that inter-rater agreement was not calculated.
estimates.moderator_quote: This cross-sectional study conducted a search on https://www.youtube.com/on February 13, 2020, using the keywords "epidural injection," "epidural steroid injection," "epidural transforaminal injection," and "epidural transforaminal steroid injection." Inclusion criteria for videos were 1) primary content related to ESI and 2) English language. [...] The 50 most-viewed videos satisfying the above criteria were included in the review.
estimates.notes: Coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY because the misleading label requires at least one inaccurate statement judged against a named clinical guideline, so a wholly accurate video cannot receive it. Rank-truncated top-50 within a single-topic keyword corpus, hence denom_scope topical with denom_selection curated. No country is stated for the videos; only the language filter is. Source-type detail worth noting: three of the four misleading videos were made by patients (all three patient-produced videos were misleading), the fourth by a media organisation; none of the 41 hospital or physician videos was misleading.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language YouTube videos; authors based in the Republic of Korea)
estimates.measure_type: % of the 50 most-viewed YouTube videos on epidural steroid injection rated highly reliable (modified DISCERN score of 3 or more)
estimates.value_raw: 22% (n = 11) with mDISCERN >= 3 (score distribution 5: n=1; 4: n=1; 3: n=9; 2: n=18; 1: n=1; 0: n=20); mean mDISCERN 1.5 (SD 1.3, range 0-5)
estimates.denominator: the same 50 most-viewed English-language YouTube videos on epidural steroid injection
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if it scored 3 or more on the modified DISCERN scale, whose five items ask whether the aims are clear and achieved, reliable sources are used, the information is balanced and unbiased, additional sources are listed, and areas of uncertainty are mentioned.
estimates.misinfo_def: No definition of misinformation is given; mDISCERN measures reliability of presentation and sourcing, not veracity.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two physiatrist authors scored every video, discrepancies resolved by discussion; no inter-rater agreement statistic was calculated, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation.
estimates.moderator_quote: The reliability of video content was assessed using the modified DISCERN scale (mDISCERN) [...] When a mDISCERN score is 3 or greater, the information is highly reliable.
estimates.notes: The quote is the Table 1 row; the Results text says 'Of these videos, 22% (n = 11) contained information with high reliability (mDISCERN score: 5, n = 1; 4, n = 1; 3, n = 9; 2, n = 18; 1, n = 1; 0, n = 20)', which the text file renders with '11' split as '1 1'. QUALITY row, to be excluded from prevalence: a low mDISCERN score means poor sourcing and balance, not falsity, and a wholly accurate video can score 0. The value recorded is the share rated highly reliable; the share NOT highly reliable (78%) would be a computed complement and is not entered. All 11 highly reliable videos were produced by hospitals or physicians; no media-organisation or patient video reached the threshold.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language YouTube videos; authors based in the Republic of Korea)
estimates.measure_type: % of the 50 most-viewed YouTube videos on epidural steroid injection of moderate to excellent quality (Global Quality Scale of 3 or more)
estimates.value_raw: 34% (n = 17): moderate n = 11 (22%), good n = 2 (4%), excellent n = 4 (8%); poor 44% (n = 22) and generally poor 22% (n = 11); mean GQS 2.3 (SD 1.1, range 1-5)
estimates.denominator: the same 50 most-viewed English-language YouTube videos on epidural steroid injection
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if it scored 3 or more on the five-point Global Quality Scale, which rates flow, coverage and usefulness of the information for patients rather than its accuracy.
estimates.misinfo_def: No definition of misinformation is given; GQS measures the completeness and usability of the information, not its veracity.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two physiatrist authors scored every video, discrepancies resolved by discussion; no inter-rater agreement statistic was calculated.
estimates.moderator_quote: The Global Quality Scale (GQS) was used for assessing the quality of video content. This evaluation tool was originally developed to evaluate website resources and assess the flow and ease of use of the information available.
estimates.notes: The quote is the Table 1 row; the Results text says 'Regarding assessment of information quality, 17 videos (34%) were of moderate (n = 11, 22%), good (n = 2, 4%), or excellent (n = 4, 8%) quality. Conversely, 44% (n = 22) and 22% (n = 11) were of poor and generally poor quality, respectively', which the text file renders with stray spaces inside words and numbers. QUALITY row, to be excluded from prevalence. A poor GQS score signals missing or badly organised information, which a wholly accurate video can receive, so this is not a falsity measure.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The 'useful' arm of the same three-way classification (76%, n = 38) and the 'neither useful nor misleading' arm (16%, n = 8) were not given their own rows: they come from the one instrument whose misleading arm is already extracted, and usefulness is a QUALITY concept under the review's rules. Both counts are recorded inside the CONTENT row's value_raw. (2) Source-type breakdowns of the misleading videos were not made into rows because the denominators are tiny and the paper's headline is the overall figure: all 41 hospital/physician videos were useful (34) or neither (7) and none misleading; of six media-organisation videos, four useful, one misleading, one neither; all three patient videos were misleading. The last of these is a 3/3 = 100% share on n = 3, which would be a misleading datapoint to enter into any synthesis. (3) Quality by production source (hospital/physician GQS >= 3 in 14/41 = 34.1%; media organisations 3/6 = 50%) is a QUALITY subgroup of an already-recorded QUALITY row. (4) View, like, dislike and subscriber counts are reported as means with no misinformation denominator, so no exposure or reach row is possible; the significance tests comparing engagement across quality bands are not prevalence estimates. (5) No inter-rater reliability was computed, which the authors state as a limitation and which weakens all three rows equally.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Frame: YouTube searched on 13 February 2020 on four ESI keywords; inclusion required primary content on ESI and English language; duplicates and videos without audio excluded; the 50 most-viewed qualifying videos retained (no random sampling, no ads, no view weighting). Instruments: modified DISCERN (5 items, threshold >= 3 for high reliability), Global Quality Scale (5 points, threshold >= 3), and a three-way useful / misleading / neither classification. Coding by the two authors, both rehabilitation physicians, with discrepancies discussed to consensus and assessment anchored to the Spine Intervention Society practice guidelines. Reliability: none reported; the authors write 'our study is limited, in that we did not calculate inter-rater agreement'. Analysis: Mann-Whitney U tests on video features. Ethics approval not required.
